title: Diagnose Windows issues
summary: Use evidence before changing a working system.

passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: Slow performance and crashes describe symptoms rather than causes. First establish what changed, which users are affected, when the issue began, and whether it can be reproduced. Task Manager can reveal resource pressure and a process consuming CPU, memory, or disk activity. Event logs can provide timestamps and error context. Correlate those observations with the reported problem instead of treating every warning in a log as the cause.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: A startup issue may involve firmware boot selection, storage access, system files, or a recent driver change. Record the exact error and use the least disruptive suitable diagnostic path. A recent update is a useful clue, not proof of causation. Before rollback or repair, consider the user’s data, recovery keys, backup status, and authorization. Test one change at a time so the result remains interpretable. After an apparent fix, repeat the original task and check related functionality; a computer merely reaching the desktop does not prove the user’s issue is resolved.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
